lines.text: A mountain island of sugar, rebellion and song. This is Jamaica, from the Taino and the Maroons to reggae and the fastest runners on Earth.
Long before Europeans came, the Taino lived here, as they did across the great islands of the Caribbean.
Spain took the island in 1509, but in 1655 Britain seized it, and would rule for three centuries.
As the Spanish fled, Africans escaped slavery into the hills. These Maroons lived free and fought to stay that way.
In 1692 an earthquake sank much of Port Royal, the richest pirate haven of the Caribbean, into the sea.
Across the harbour, survivors built a new town, Kingston, which became the capital.
Sugar was worked by enslaved Africans. In 1831 they rose in the great Baptist War, and within a few years slavery was ended.
In 1865 Paul Bogle led the Morant Bay rebellion against injustice, and it was put down with great cruelty.
Alexander Bustamante, a labour leader, would become the first prime minister of independent Jamaica.
Marcus Garvey, born on the north coast, would lead a worldwide movement for Black pride.
Norman Manley founded the People's National Party, and is remembered as a father of independence.
His son, Michael Manley, would lead the country in the seventies, and again at the end of the eighties.
In the 1930s the Rastafari faith began in Jamaica, honouring Haile Selassie of Ethiopia and looking to Africa as home.
Bob Marley, born in the hills of Saint Ann, would carry Jamaica's music and its message to the whole world.
In the late fifties came ska, quick and upbeat, the music that would lead to rocksteady and then reggae.
In August 1962 Jamaica became independent, a nation of its own after three centuries of British rule.
By the late sixties reggae was born, with its off-beat guitar and heavy bass, songs of struggle, faith and unity.
Andrew Holness would lead the country as prime minister from 2016.
Usain Bolt became the fastest man in history, with world records in the hundred and two hundred metres and eight Olympic golds.
Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce matched him on the women's side, five times world champion over a hundred metres.
In 1988 a team from a land without snow went to the Winter Olympics in a bobsled, and won the world's affection.
That same year Hurricane Gilbert swept across the whole island.
And in October 2025 Hurricane Melissa, one of the strongest Atlantic storms on record, struck Jamaica.
Through storms and struggle, Jamaica has given the world its rhythm and its speed.
